questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a 2 month history of his jaw tiring halfway through meals and his speech becoming nasal and slurred by the evening. He is normal first thing in the morning. On examination there is mild bilateral ptosis. Tongue bulk is normal with no fasciculations. Reflexes and sensation are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bulbar and ocular weakness that worsens with use and through the day, with normal reflexes and sensation, is myasthenia gravis.

clues: normal first thing in the morning
steps.x: Bulbar weakness that fatigues with use and is worst in the evening, plus ptosis.

elim: Sudden onset with fixed deficits, not weakness that varies with use.
Progressive, not fatigable, with tongue wasting and fasciculations.
Mainly proximal leg weakness that improves with use, with reduced reflexes and autonomic symptoms.
Slowly progressive and familial, without day-to-day fluctuation.

steps.x: D: Myasthenia gravis. Fatigable bulbar and ocular weakness = myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: A 35 year old hairdresser has a 3 month history of her arms becoming heavy after a few minutes of blow-drying, recovering after a short rest. In the evenings she sees double when watching television. Her creatine kinase is normal. Reflexes, sensation and coordination are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Proximal limb weakness that comes on with use and recovers with rest, plus evening diplopia, with normal CK and reflexes, is myasthenia gravis.

clues: heavy after a few minutes of blow-drying
In the evenings she sees double
steps.x: Fatigable proximal weakness plus diplopia worse in the evening, normal muscle enzymes.

elim: An acute ascending weakness over days with areflexia.
Causes slow-relaxing reflexes, raised CK and no diplopia.
Relapses last days to weeks, not minutes of use; would show upper motor neurone signs.
Constant proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase, no ocular involvement.

steps.x: D: Myasthenia gravis. Weakness worse with activity, better with rest, ocular involvement = MG.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 6 week history of fluctuating double vision and difficulty climbing stairs late in the day. She is otherwise well. Her GP suspects a disorder of neuromuscular transmission and examines her arms after asking her to hold them outstretched to the side for 2 minutes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Absent reflexes that return after exercise
Progressive arm drift with normal reflexes
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis gives fatigable weakness (strength falls with sustained effort) with normal reflexes, sensation and pupils.

clues: hold them outstretched to the side for 2 minutes
steps.x: Diplopia and proximal weakness worse late in the day: sustained effort will show fatigue.

elim: A feature of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
A lower motor neurone sign of motor neurone disease.
A compressive lesion, not a neuromuscular junction disease; the pupil is spared in MG.
A spinal cord sign; MG has no sensory loss.

steps.x: C: Progressive arm drift with normal reflexes. MG: fatigable weakness, normal reflexes and sensation.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with myasthenia gravis has had a cold for 4 days. Today he is breathless, cannot count to 20 in one breath and his cough is weak. His respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Chest auscultation is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Infection has triggered a myasthenic crisis: respiratory muscle weakness causing type II respiratory failure and a weak (bovine) cough.

clues: cannot count to 20 in one breath
steps.x: Known MG, a trigger, weak cough and a rising CO2 with a clear chest.

elim: Would cause wheeze; his chest is clear.
Would cause fever, crackles or bronchial breathing.
There is no history of COPD and no wheeze.
Causes type I respiratory failure with a low CO2, not a weak cough and hypercapnia.

steps.x: D: Myasthenic crisis. MG with breathlessness, weak cough and type II failure = myasthenic crisis.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with myasthenia gravis is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasing breathlessness and difficulty swallowing her saliva. She speaks in short phrases. Her respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. The registrar asks her to cough.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: Cough productive of pink frothy sputum
Paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory whoop
questions.e: In myasthenic crisis respiratory and bulbar muscle weakness produce a weak, ineffective bovine cough with type II respiratory failure.

steps.x: Known MG with bulbar and respiratory muscle failure.

elim: Suggests croup or upper airway obstruction.
A sign of acute pulmonary oedema.
Pertussis.
Suggests asthma or COPD.

steps.x: D: Weak bovine cough. Myasthenic crisis: acute dyspnoea, type II failure, bovine cough.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with myasthenia gravis well controlled on pyridostigmine sees her GP with a chest infection and is started on clarithromycin. Three days later her ptosis and double vision are much worse and she is struggling to chew. Her other medicines are paracetamol, omeprazole and a salbutamol inhaler.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to have caused the deterioration?
questions.e: Macrolides such as clarithromycin, aminoglycosides, beta-blockers, antimalarials and lithium can all worsen myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: Sudden worsening days after a new antibiotic.

elim: Not known to worsen myasthenia gravis.
Safe in myasthenia gravis.
This is her treatment and was already controlling symptoms.
Does not affect neuromuscular transmission significantly.

steps.x: A: Clarithromycin. Macrolides and aminoglycosides worsen MG.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with ocular myasthenia gravis is travelling to sub-Saharan Africa. His travel clinic prescribes malaria prophylaxis. A week after starting it his double vision and ptosis become worse and he notices his arms tire quickly. He has not had any infection and takes no other new medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
questions.e: Antimalarials such as chloroquine are among the drugs that worsen myasthenia gravis, with beta-blockers, aminoglycosides, macrolides and lithium.

steps.x: Worsening of fatigable weakness straight after a new antimalarial.

elim: A separate paraneoplastic disease, not a sudden change after a drug.
He has had no infection and has no respiratory symptoms.
Would not be timed so closely to a new drug.
Causes neuropathy and anaemia over months.

steps.x: A: Antimalarial worsening neuromuscular transmission. Antimalarials can unmask or worsen MG.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with myasthenia gravis needs an emergency laparotomy. The anaesthetist plans a rapid sequence induction and asks the medical student how her condition will affect the depolarising muscle relaxant they intend to use.
questions.q: Which is the most likely response to suxamethonium in this patient?
questions.e: With fewer functional acetylcholine receptors, patients with MG are resistant to depolarising blockers like suxamethonium (and very sensitive to non-depolarising ones).

steps.x: Suxamethonium needs receptors to depolarise; MG has fewer.

elim: A genetic reaction linked to RYR1 mutations, not MG.
The reduced receptor number changes the response.
An inherited enzyme problem unrelated to MG.
Seen after burns, crush injury or denervation, not MG.

steps.x: D: Resistance, needing a higher dose. MG is resistant to suxamethonium: an important anaesthetic point.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man is diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis after a positive acetylcholine receptor antibody test. A CT chest shows a 4 cm well-defined anterior mediastinal mass. He has no weight loss, night sweats or lymphadenopathy, and his thyroid is not enlarged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the mass?
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma, which CT chest is done to look for.

clues: no weight loss, night sweats or lymphadenopathy
steps.x: An anterior mediastinal mass in MG.

elim: Usually comes with B symptoms or lymphadenopathy, and is not linked to MG.
His thyroid is not enlarged.
A germ cell tumour of young adults, not associated with MG.
Lies in the middle mediastinum and is not linked to MG.

steps.x: E: Thymoma. MG + anterior mediastinal mass = thymoma until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with myasthenia gravis controlled on pyridostigmine has a 4 month history of tiredness, weight gain, constipation and feeling cold. Her ptosis is no worse. She is not on steroids.
questions.q: Which is the most likely associated condition?
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune conditions such as hypothyroidism.

clues: weight gain, constipation and feeling cold
steps.x: Classic hypothyroid symptoms in a patient with an autoimmune disease.

elim: She is not on steroids and has no other Cushingoid features.
A paraneoplastic disease, does not explain cold intolerance or constipation.
Her myasthenic symptoms are no worse and she has no breathlessness.
She is not on steroids.

steps.x: A: Autoimmune hypothyroidism. MG comes with other autoimmune disease, especially thyroid disease.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has a 3 week history of double vision and drooping eyelids. His wife says the drooping swaps between eyes and is worse by teatime. His pupils are equal and reactive. He has no headache, jaw pain or limb weakness. His blood glucose is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Variable ptosis that changes side and is worse later in the day, with diplopia and normal pupils, is ocular myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: Fluctuating, fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils.

elim: His glucose is normal and a third nerve palsy does not swap sides or vary through the day.
Would come with headache, jaw claudication and raised inflammatory markers.
Causes mild ptosis with a small pupil on the same side, not diplopia.
Causes a painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy.

steps.x: D: Ocular myasthenia gravis. Variable ptosis and diplopia worse in the evening, pupils spared = MG.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 2 month history of ptosis and diplopia worse in the evening and difficulty lifting her arms to wash her hair. Her neurologist explains that the cause is an autoimmune problem at the junction between nerve and muscle.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
o: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis is caused by IgG autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, impairing transmission.

clues: ptosis and diplopia worse in the evening
autoimmune problem at the junction between nerve and muscle
steps.x: Fatigable ocular and limb weakness from an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease.

elim: Cause Guillain-Barré and Miller Fisher syndromes.
Cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
Causes descending paralysis with fixed dilated pupils.
Motor neurone disease is degenerative, not autoimmune.

steps.x: C: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors. MG: IgG against postsynaptic AChR.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has a 2 month history of rapidly worsening weakness of her face, tongue and neck. She now has trouble swallowing and her head drops forward by the afternoon. Her eye movements are only mildly affected. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. Muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibodies are positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: MuSK antibodies are linked to a more severe, progressive form of MG with marked bulbar, neck and respiratory involvement.

clues: rapidly worsening weakness of her face, tongue and neck
Muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibodies are positive
steps.x: Severe bulbar and neck weakness with MuSK rather than AChR antibodies.

elim: Would show fasciculations and is not antibody mediated.
Mainly affects proximal legs with voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies.
An inherited myopathy with myotonia and frontal balding.
Confined to the eyes; she has severe bulbar and neck weakness.

steps.x: C: MuSK antibody-positive myasthenia gravis. MuSK MG: more severe, bulbar-predominant.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a 5 week history of double vision that he only notices when driving home from work. His GP asks him to look up at her finger for a minute without blinking. His pupils are equal and reactive and eye movements look full at the start of the test.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding during the test?
questions.e: Sustained upgaze brings out fatigable ptosis in myasthenia gravis; ptosis and diplopia worsen as the day goes on.

clues: only notices when driving home from work
look up at her finger for a minute
steps.x: Diplopia late in the day, normal pupils: test for fatigability.

elim: A third nerve compression sign, not fatigue.
A sign of thyrotoxicosis.
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia from an MLF lesion.
MG weakness gets worse, not better, with use.

steps.x: A: Eyelids gradually droop. MG: ptosis develops on sustained upgaze.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has a 2 month history of double vision and drooping eyelids by the evening, and his arms tire when shaving. Reflexes and sensation are normal. His GP refers him to neurology, who want to confirm the suspected diagnosis with a blood test before anything else.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: The first-line test for suspected MG is an acetylcholine receptor antibody screen (with anti-MuSK antibodies).

steps.x: Fatigable ocular and limb weakness: suspected MG.

elim: Raised in myositis, normal in MG.
A historic bedside test, now rarely used because of cardiac risks.
Used to look for central causes of diplopia, not to confirm MG.
Test for Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

steps.x: A: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Suspected MG: AChR antibody screen first.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has a 3 month history of fatigable ptosis, difficulty swallowing and neck weakness. Reflexes and sensation are normal. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. Her neurologist still suspects an autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: The antibody screen includes anti-MuSK antibodies; AChR-negative patients with bulbar weakness often have MuSK MG, a more severe form.

steps.x: AChR-negative but clinically MG, with bulbar and neck weakness.

elim: Test for Miller Fisher syndrome, an acute post-infective neuropathy.
Screen for lupus and connective tissue disease.
Used for CNS infection or inflammation, not MG.
Used for myopathies, not neuromuscular junction disease.

steps.x: B: Anti-MuSK antibodies. AChR antibodies negative: test anti-MuSK.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has fatigable ptosis, diplopia and proximal arm weakness. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are pending. Neurophysiology studies are arranged, including repetitive stimulation of a motor nerve at 3 Hz while recording from the muscle.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on repetitive nerve stimulation?
questions.e: In MG repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response: each muscle action potential is smaller than the last.

clues: repetitive stimulation of a motor nerve
steps.x: Fatigable weakness on a neurophysiology test means the response falls with repetition.

elim: Show denervation, as in motor neurone disease.
Typical of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
Seen in myotonic dystrophy.
Shows a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy.

steps.x: A: Decremental response. MG on EMG: decremental response to repetitive stimulation.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has suspected myasthenia gravis. A visiting consultant suggests giving intravenous edrophonium and watching whether her ptosis improves. The registrar says that an antibody test is preferred and that edrophonium is now rarely used.
questions.q: Which is the main reason the edrophonium test is rarely used?
o: It is only positive in MuSK disease
It takes several weeks to give a result
Risk of bradycardia and other cardiac complications
questions.e: The edrophonium (Tensilon) test is a historic diagnostic test, rarely used now because of cardiac risks such as bradycardia; the AChR antibody screen is the initial test.

steps.x: A short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor causes cholinergic effects on the heart.

elim: It can be positive in any MG with acetylcholine receptor failure.
It is a bedside intravenous test.
The effect is seen within minutes.
No contrast is involved.

steps.x: E: Risk of bradycardia and other cardiac complications. Tensilon test: historic, cardiac risk; use antibodies instead.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has just been diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis. Her acetylcholine receptor antibodies are strongly positive and she has started pyridostigmine with good effect. She asks whether anything else needs to be checked.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Once MG is diagnosed, CT chest looks for an underlying thymoma.

clues: just been diagnosed with generalised myasthenia gravis
anything else needs to be checked
steps.x: New MG: look for the associated thymic tumour.

elim: No cardiac symptoms; not part of MG work-up.
MG is a neuromuscular junction disease; brain imaging is not needed.
Not needed once antibodies confirm MG.
Does not look at the thymus.

steps.x: A: CT chest. After diagnosing MG: CT chest for thymoma.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with myasthenia gravis is admitted with a chest infection, worsening ptosis and a weak voice. She says she feels a little short of breath. Her respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The ward team want to monitor her for respiratory failure.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor her respiratory effort?
questions.e: FVC is the gold standard for monitoring respiratory effort in myasthenic crisis; saturations can be normal until late.

steps.x: Possible evolving crisis with normal saturations.

elim: Changes in gases are late; respiratory muscle weakness shows first in FVC.
Shows the infection, not respiratory muscle strength.
Stays normal until respiratory failure is advanced.
Measures airway obstruction, not neuromuscular weakness.

steps.x: C: Forced vital capacity. MG respiratory monitoring: serial FVC, not saturations.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a 4 month history of ptosis and diplopia that are worse in the evening and his arms tire when painting a ceiling. Reflexes and sensation are normal. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies and anti-MuSK antibodies are both negative.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to support the diagnosis?
questions.e: In seronegative MG, repetitive nerve stimulation (EMG) showing a decremental response supports the diagnosis.

steps.x: Clinically MG, antibodies negative: test neuromuscular transmission directly.

elim: Normal in MG; helps with myositis.
Looks for CNS infection or inflammation.
Would not explain fatigable ocular weakness.
Normal in MG; repetitive stimulation is needed.

steps.x: E: Repetitive nerve stimulation. Seronegative MG: repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decrement.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has a 2 month history of drooping eyelids and double vision in the evenings. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and CT chest is normal. He has no bulbar or limb symptoms and finds the double vision is stopping him from reading.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Pyridostigmine, a long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is first-line treatment for MG.

steps.x: Newly confirmed MG without crisis.

elim: A steroid-sparing immunosuppressant for persistent symptoms, not first line.
Used for myasthenic crisis.
Used for myasthenic crisis.
His CT chest is normal and he is elderly with ocular disease.

steps.x: D: Pyridostigmine. MG first line: pyridostigmine.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis has persistent symptoms despite pyridostigmine. She started prednisolone 6 months ago with good effect, but her symptoms return whenever the dose is reduced below 20 mg. She has now developed osteoporosis and raised blood glucose.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Persistent symptoms are treated with prednisolone and/or azathioprine; azathioprine allows the steroid dose to be reduced.

clues: return whenever the dose is reduced
steps.x: Steroid-dependent MG with steroid side effects.

elim: Beta-blockers worsen MG.
Kept for crisis, not a steroid-sparing plan.
This would worsen symptoms.
Thymectomy is for thymoma or selected cases after imaging, not a steroid-sparing step here.

steps.x: A: Add azathioprine. Second line in MG: prednisolone and/or azathioprine.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man with acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis is improving on pyridostigmine and prednisolone. His staging CT chest shows a 3 cm encapsulated anterior mediastinal mass. He is fit and well otherwise.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Thymectomy is the definitive treatment, particularly where thymoma is present, because the thymus drives autoantibody production.

steps.x: MG with a resectable thymoma.

elim: Not first line for an encapsulated thymoma.
Used for crisis; it does not treat the thymoma.
Not the first definitive treatment for a resectable thymoma.
A thymoma in MG should be removed.

steps.x: E: Thymectomy. MG with thymoma: thymectomy.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with myasthenia gravis is admitted with a chest infection and increasing difficulty swallowing. His forced vital capacity has been measured every 4 hours (see item resources). He is now speaking in short sentences and his oxygen saturation is 95% on 2 L/min oxygen.

visual.title: Forced vital capacity
visual.caption: FVC is falling steadily towards the level at which ventilation is needed.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase the oxygen to 15 L/min and observe
Refer to critical care for intubation and ventilation
questions.e: A steadily falling FVC in myasthenic crisis means impending ventilatory failure: admit for respiratory support, which may need intubation and ventilation.

steps.x: FVC is falling fast during a crisis: the muscles of breathing are failing.

elim: He is in evolving crisis and needs respiratory support.
Takes months to work and does nothing for the airway now.
Oxygen does not fix ventilatory failure from weak muscles.
There is no bronchospasm.

steps.x: D: Refer to critical care for intubation and ventilation. Falling FVC in myasthenic crisis: secure ventilation early.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman with myasthenia gravis is in the intensive care unit with a myasthenic crisis triggered by pneumonia. She is intubated and ventilated and receiving antibiotics. IV immunoglobulin is not available in the hospital today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Myasthenic crisis is treated definitively with IV immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis, plus respiratory support.

steps.x: Crisis with ventilation secured; the alternative to IVIG is needed.

elim: Takes months to work; not for crisis.
Not done during a crisis.
Not the definitive acute treatment for crisis.
Do not treat neuromuscular weakness.

steps.x: C: Plasma exchange. Myasthenic crisis: IVIG or plasma exchange.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with myasthenia gravis is on the surgical ward with a urinary tract infection after a hernia repair. He was started on IV gentamicin 24 hours ago. Since then his ptosis has worsened and his voice has become weak. His FVC is 2.9 L and stable and he is not breathless.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop gentamicin and change to another antibiotic
questions.e: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin worsen MG; stop the drug, use a safer antibiotic and monitor FVC.

steps.x: Worsening MG straight after an aminoglycoside, without respiratory failure.

elim: Beta-blockers also worsen MG.
Thymectomy is not a treatment for a drug-induced worsening.
Gentamicin is causing the deterioration and could precipitate crisis.
His FVC is stable and he is not breathless.

steps.x: E: Stop gentamicin and change to another antibiotic. Aminoglycosides worsen MG: stop them.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis after positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies. During a teaching session the consultant asks how her disease would be classified by the Gell and Coombs system, given that the antibodies bind a receptor on the cell surface.
questions.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
o: Mixed type I and type IV
questions.e: MG is a type II hypersensitivity reaction: IgG autoantibodies bind postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

clues: bind a receptor on the cell surface
steps.x: IgG against a fixed cell-surface antigen.

elim: MG is not IgE or T-cell effector mediated; the damage is done by IgG against a cell-surface receptor.
IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity, such as anaphylaxis.
Immune complex deposition, such as lupus nephritis.
Delayed T-cell-mediated, such as contact dermatitis.

steps.x: C: Type II. Antibody against a cell-surface receptor = type II.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has myasthenia gravis with positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Electron microscopy of a neuromuscular junction from a research biopsy shows a simplified, flattened postsynaptic membrane with few receptors.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the reduced receptor number?
o: Blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Mutations in the receptor subunit genes
Receptor internalisation and complement-mediated membrane damage
questions.e: Antibody binding causes receptor internalisation and complement-mediated destruction of the postsynaptic membrane, reducing functional receptor number.

clues: flattened postsynaptic membrane with few receptors
steps.x: Antibodies on the postsynaptic membrane: receptors lost and membrane damaged.

elim: The mechanism of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
Not the mechanism of MG.
Congenital myasthenic syndromes, not autoimmune MG.
The problem is on the postsynaptic side.

steps.x: D: Receptor internalisation and complement-mediated membrane damage. MG: antibodies cause internalisation and complement damage.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with myasthenia gravis can grip the examiner's hand strongly at first, but after repeated grips the strength falls away. After 2 minutes of rest her grip strength recovers.
questions.q: Which best explains why her weakness worsens with repeated use?
o: Acetylcholine release falls with repeated firing while receptors are reduced
Lactic acid builds up in the muscle
Motor neurones die with repeated firing
Muscle fibres are replaced by fat
Sodium channels are blocked by antibodies
questions.e: Repeated stimulation depletes available acetylcholine relative to the reduced receptor pool, so transmission fails and strength falls until rest.

clues: after repeated grips the strength falls away
steps.x: Weakness with repetition that recovers with rest: transmission is failing.

elim: Normal fatigue, not the cause of myasthenic fatigability.
Neurones do not die with use.
A feature of muscular dystrophies, which do not recover with rest.
Not the MG mechanism.

steps.x: A: Acetylcholine release falls with repeated firing while receptors are reduced. Fatigability = falling ACh release meeting too few receptors.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has severe bulbar weakness and has needed ventilatory support twice. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative but anti-MuSK antibodies are positive. A student asks why this form of the disease behaves differently.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of disease in this patient?
o: Antibody blockade of presynaptic calcium channels
questions.e: MuSK antibodies impair clustering of acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic membrane, often causing more severe bulbar and respiratory involvement.

steps.x: MuSK organises receptor clusters; without clustering, transmission fails.

elim: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
Motor neurone disease.
Not the mechanism of MuSK MG.
Botulism.

steps.x: D: Impaired clustering of acetylcholine receptors. MuSK antibodies stop AChR clustering: more severe bulbar disease.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive myasthenia gravis and thymic hyperplasia on CT is offered thymectomy. She asks how removing a gland in her chest can help a disease of her muscles.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: The thymus compresses the phrenic nerves
The thymus releases a muscle toxin
questions.e: Thymic hyperplasia or thymoma is thought to drive autoantibody production, so thymectomy reduces the autoimmune attack.

clues: how removing a gland in her chest can help
steps.x: The thymus is where the autoimmune response is thought to start.

elim: Weakness is generalised and not due to compression.
It does not.
There is no such toxin.
Acetylcholine is made in motor nerve terminals.

steps.x: B: The thymus drives autoantibody production. Thymectomy removes the driver of autoantibody production.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man with myasthenia gravis starts pyridostigmine. Within an hour of each dose his ptosis improves, even though his antibody level has not changed. He asks why the tablet helps when the antibodies are still there.
questions.q: Which best explains the improvement?
o: Acetylcholine stays longer in the synaptic cleft
Antibodies are removed from the circulation
questions.e: Pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, prolonging acetylcholine's action in the cleft and partly compensating for reduced receptor density.

steps.x: It works quickly without changing the antibodies, so it acts on the synapse.

elim: This is plasma exchange.
Pyridostigmine does not increase receptor number.
Not the action of pyridostigmine.
This is the action of immunosuppressants such as azathioprine.

steps.x: A: Acetylcholine stays longer in the synaptic cleft. Pyridostigmine prolongs ACh action at the NMJ.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with myasthenia gravis controlled on pyridostigmine is found to have new atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 118 bpm. Her BP is 134/82 mmHg. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 4. The ward pharmacist reviews the drugs the team has suggested starting.
questions.q: Which of the proposed drugs should be avoided?
questions.e: Beta-blockers worsen myasthenia gravis, as do aminoglycosides, macrolides, antimalarials and lithium, so choose another rate-control drug.

steps.x: Rate control is needed, but one common choice worsens MG.

elim: An anticoagulant that does not affect neuromuscular transmission and is indicated with a score of 4.
Can be used for rate control without worsening MG.
Safe in MG.
Not known to worsen MG.

steps.x: B: Bisoprolol. Avoid beta-blockers in MG.
